name: Dutasteride mesotherapy

lead: Dutasteride mesotherapy delivers dutasteride, a drug that blocks the conversion of testosterone to DHT, into the scalp through many small intradermal injections instead of as a capsule. It is used off-label for androgenetic alopecia and appeals to people who want the effect acting locally on the scalp.

The chain is local DHT reduction: dutasteride inhibits type 1, 2 and 3 5-alpha reductase, and DHT is linked to follicle miniaturisation in pattern hair loss, so lowering it slows loss and may improve density. Proponents say depositing it in the skin keeps systemic absorption low. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 33 studies included it as a comparator, a randomised comparison of monthly versus quarterly sessions was published in 2026 as a letter, and case series exist.

paras: Clinicians perform repeated sessions with a manual needle or multi-needle device, typically spaced weeks to months apart, and it is often combined with other hair treatments.

Dutasteride is not approved for hair loss in the US, and mesotherapy with it is unapproved. Case series from 2024 to 2026 report non-scarring and persistent alopecia, and anagen effluvium, at injection sites. A 2026 review notes compounded injectables can contain different excipients, some linked to complement-activation reactions. Oral dutasteride carries a label with sexual and other warnings.

chain: Hair loss slows, density may improve
angle.text: Clinicians inject dilute dutasteride into the scalp to reduce local DHT, slowing hair loss and possibly improving density. It is an off-label alternative to oral dutasteride or finasteride, backed by small early trials and case reports.

lead: Dutasteride mesotherapy is the off-label practice of injecting dilute dutasteride, a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, into the scalp skin in multiple small intradermal deposits to treat androgenetic alopecia (AGA, or pattern hair loss). It is performed by clinicians, sometimes with a manual needle or a multi-needle device, and is discussed in hair-loss communities as an alternative to oral dutasteride or finasteride. [1][2]

Dutasteride itself is approved in the US for benign prostatic hyperplasia and is prescribed off-label for hair loss. It is approved for male pattern hair loss in South Korea, Japan and Taiwan. [3] The Food and Drug Administration has not approved dutasteride mesotherapy. [4]

Published evidence is limited. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 33 studies included dutasteride mesotherapy as one of its comparators alongside oral and topical minoxidil, finasteride and dutasteride. [1] A randomized trial comparing monthly with quarterly sessions was published in 2026 as a letter, and a case series (2024) reported outcomes in treated patients. [5][6] Meanwhile, several case series describe hair loss occurring at the injection sites. [4][7][8]
infobox: Not approved by the FDA for this use

paras: Mesotherapy is a technique in which practitioners inject drugs, vitamins or other substances into or just under the skin. The term came from the French press in 1958, and Michel Pistor is credited as its founder. [9] In hair-loss care the approach is applied by delivering a dilute drug solution across the scalp.

In one published case series, a clinic administered 2 ml of 0.01 percent dutasteride monthly in small grid-based intradermal deposits. [4] Published protocols and formulations differ, and compounded products vary between pharmacies. [2]

Dutasteride inhibits both type 1 and type 2 isoenzymes of 5-alpha reductase, which convert testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). [4] Wikipedia describes it as inhibiting all three forms and lowering circulating DHT by up to about 98 percent when taken orally, with a half-life of roughly four to five weeks. [3]

Authors of the clinical literature describe the rationale for intradermal delivery as depositing the drug locally with negligible systemic absorption, reducing the systemic exposure associated with oral 5-alpha reductase inhibitors. [4][6]

A 2017 survey of 241 dermatologists in Spain found oral dutasteride prescribed for male pattern hair loss by about a third of respondents, with topical and oral finasteride and minoxidil far more common, and many treatments used off-label. [10] The survey predates the wider use of dutasteride mesotherapy and does not measure it.

A 2025 network meta-analysis in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology identified 33 eligible studies and 19 comparators, which included minoxidil (oral, topical, sublingual), finasteride (oral, topical, mesotherapy) and dutasteride (oral, mesotherapy). It compared changes in total and terminal hair density at 24 and 48 weeks and a 24-week independent observer assessment. [1]

A randomized trial comparing monthly with quarterly dutasteride mesotherapy sessions in men with androgenetic alopecia was published as a letter in the Journal of the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology in 2026. [5] A 2024 case series in JAAD Case Reports described outcomes in patients treated with dutasteride mesotherapy. [6]

A phase 4 trial registered in 2023 (NCT06110377, n=60, status unknown) compares dutasteride mesotherapy delivered by standard injection with injections delivered by a tattoo machine in men with androgenetic alopecia. [11]

A 2025 case series in the International Journal of Trichology described 15 patients with patterned hair loss (13 men and 2 women) who received monthly dutasteride mesotherapy; several developed non-scarring alopecia after a single session. [4]

A 2026 case series in the Journal of Drugs in Dermatology reported three women with persistent alopecic patches after dutasteride mesotherapy, and noted that alopecia at injection sites has been increasingly reported. [7] A 2026 report in Actas Dermo-Sifiliograficas describes three cases of anagen effluvium attributed to the procedure. [8]

A 2026 review of complement activation-related pseudoallergy notes that intralesional dutasteride is increasingly used in dermatology, that vehicles differ among manufacturers and compounding pharmacies, and that some excipients, such as Cremophor EL, have been implicated in complement-mediated reactions. [2]

More generally, reported problems with mesotherapy include skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection at an Australian salon. [9] Oral dutasteride's label and the literature describe sexual side effects and a 2011 FDA warning about high-grade prostate cancer in BPH trials. [3]

The FDA has not approved dutasteride for mesotherapy. [4] Dutasteride is prescription-only in the United States and United Kingdom. [3] For mesotherapy in general, the only injectable the FDA has approved for a cosmetic use is deoxycholic acid for submental fat, and some countries have restricted the technique. [9]

timeline.event: The term mesotherapy appears in the French press. [9]
FDA approves dutasteride for benign prostatic hyperplasia. [3]
Dutasteride approved for hair loss in South Korea. [3]
A phase 4 trial of dutasteride mesotherapy techniques registers. [11]
Case series of outcomes with dutasteride mesotherapy published. [6]
Network meta-analysis includes dutasteride mesotherapy; case series report paradoxical alopecia. [1][4]
Randomized monthly-versus-quarterly trial letter and further case reports of injection-site hair loss appear. [5][7][8]
